presentation.title: The Free Mint problem
presentation.text: The website says, Free Mint. But the request underneath can give someone permission to move every NFT in a collection. I'm Mohamed Adib, a student at Sri Venkateswara College of Engineering. This is PlainSign: a way to understand that permission before approving it.

presentation.title: Before the wallet opens
presentation.text: Here is the permission in this test example. PlainSign pauses the request and shows the address that would get access. It explains why that permission is dangerous. If I choose Reject, it returns the wallet's standard rejection error. The request never reaches the wallet. The Continue button forwards the original request unchanged. The separate demo shows that interception working.

presentation.title: Signatures matter too
presentation.text: A signature with no gas fee still deserves attention. This Permit2 example grants an unlimited token permission for a long time. A normal sign-in message has a different meaning. PlainSign decodes both and shows the difference. Green means no major warning signs were found under the rules; it is not a guarantee of safety.

presentation.title: Open rules, visible reasons
presentation.text: The decision comes from open rules. We decode the transaction or signature, add public chain information, and explain the rules that fired. This public version does not use AI to write the explanation. It has no backend account or telemetry. These are inspectable heuristics, and provider interception is best effort.

presentation.title: Work completed for the event
presentation.text: The September prototype came before this competition, and that history is disclosed. The October work adds public contract data from the main Ethereum network. It keeps warnings about known malicious addresses visible during an RPC outage. It also gives judges a walkthrough they can try without a wallet. The walkthrough uses simulated metadata. Mainnet validation uses public reads, not real asset transactions.

presentation.title: The business hypothesis
presentation.text: For individuals, the extension and rules stay free and open source. The proposed business is a software package that wallets and apps can add to their products. It would include maintained rules, policy controls, and support. I still need to test demand and pricing. I am not claiming customers or revenue today.

presentation.title: The next proof
presentation.text: The next test is simple: watch five people use the demo. Can they explain the permission before deciding? Where do warnings confuse them? How long does the decision take? Then I want to find two wallet or app teams for a small integration pilot. Those are planned experiments, not current traction.

presentation.title: PlainSign
presentation.text: The goal is to help people make a clear decision at the moment it matters. You can try the sample requests without installing a wallet, and inspect the code and rules in the repository. My next milestones are independent security review and observed user tests. PlainSign helps people understand the permission, then decide.

demo.title: Controlled demo
demo.text: This is PlainSign running in a controlled test. The extension is real; the wallet is automated and the chain metadata is simulated. No real assets move. CatDrop is a security-training page with deliberately risky examples.

demo.title: Connect
demo.text: I connect the disposable test account. The notice makes clear that this is a fictional offer. Each supported request passes through PlainSign before it can reach the wallet.

demo.title: Free Mint
demo.text: Free Mint actually requests permission to move every NFT in this collection. PlainSign marks the request as dangerous. It shows the address that would get access. The reasons explain why permission over the whole collection is risky. This is the permission the button's label hides.

demo.title: Reject
demo.text: I choose Reject. The page reports error four zero zero one. The test wallet receives no signing or transaction request for this action. That lets me stop before forwarding the permission.

demo.title: Permit2
demo.text: Now, Sign to verify wallet. This is a Permit2 signature with an unlimited amount and a long expiry. PlainSign flags the permission and shows Danger. There is no gas fee for signing, but the signature can still allow assets to move later. I reject it.

demo.title: Sign in
demo.text: The sign-in example gets a different explanation. The decoded message is a login rather than an asset permission. It receives Safe under these rules. That verdict does not tell us that the website itself is trustworthy.

demo.title: Wrap ETH
demo.text: The wrapped Ether deposit explains the exchange of Ether for wrapped Ether. This controlled example also receives Safe. I reject the request here, so no transaction is sent. Optional simulation supports Sepolia only.

demo.title: Try it yourself
demo.text: Judges can compare these requests in the sample walkthrough without a wallet or extension. It uses the same decoder and rules, with simulated metadata clearly labelled. The repository includes the development history and the work added during this event.
